explanations.explanation_text: In anaerobic glycolysis, 4 ATP are generated at substrate level (by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase) and 2 ATP are consumed in the preparatory phase (by hexokinase and PFK-1), yielding a net gain of exactly 2 ATP per glucose molecule. The 2 NADH produced are re-oxidized by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+, so no ETC ATP is formed. Under aerobic conditions, re-oxidation of 2 cytosolic NADH by the ETC yields up to 5 ATP, but under anaerobic conditions NADH cannot be oxidized by mitochondria. Four ATP represents the gross substrate-level ATP generation before subtracting the 2 ATP invested in the activation reactions. Incorrect: Seven ATP represents the net energy yield of aerobic glycolysis (4 substrate ATP + 5 ETC ATP - 2 consumed ATP = 7 ATP).

explanations.explanation_text: In anaerobic glycolysis, 4 ATP are generated at substrate level (by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase) and 2 ATP are consumed in the preparatory phase (by hexokinase and PFK-1), yielding a net gain of exactly 2 ATP per glucose molecule. The 2 NADH produced are re-oxidized by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+, so no ETC ATP is formed. Under aerobic conditions, re-oxidation of 2 cytosolic NADH by the ETC yields up to 5 ATP, but under anaerobic conditions NADH cannot be oxidized by mitochondria. Four ATP represents the gross substrate-level ATP generation before subtracting the 2 ATP invested in the activation reactions. Incorrect: Seven ATP represents the net energy yield of aerobic glycolysis (4 substrate ATP + 5 ETC ATP - 2 consumed ATP = 7 ATP).

explanations.source_document: Physio - القسم.pdf, pp. 13-14

explanations.explanation_text: Tryptophan is mixed (both glucogenic and ketogenic).
explanations.source_document: NS 101 2027 part(1) Bio.pdf, printed p. 32 (PDF p. 34)

explanations.explanation_text: Isoleucine is mixed (both glucogenic and ketogenic).
explanations.source_document: NS 101 2027 part(1) Bio.pdf, printed p. 32 (PDF p. 34)

explanations.explanation_text: Tyrosine is mixed (both glucogenic and ketogenic).
explanations.source_document: NS 101 2027 part(1) Bio.pdf, printed p. 32 (PDF p. 34)

explanations.explanation_text: Methionine is catabolized to propionyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA (TCA cycle intermediate) to generate glucose, making it purely glucogenic.
explanations.source_document: NS 101 2027 part(1) Bio.pdf, printed p. 32 (PDF p. 34)

explanations.explanation_text: While CO2 exchange is carried out by erythrocytes, the primary histological adaptation of enucleation is maximizing internal space for hemoglobin packing.
explanations.source_document: Histo - القسم.pdf, p. 8; Physio - القسم.pdf, p. 7

explanations.explanation_text: Enucleated mature red blood cells cannot undergo cell division; they are post-mitotic cells derived from nucleated bone marrow progenitors.
explanations.source_document: Histo - القسم.pdf, pp. 5, 21-22

explanations.explanation_text: Non-heme iron present in cereals, vegetables, and plant sources contains phytic acid, which binds iron into insoluble chelates, making it non-absorbable and poorly bioavailable.
explanations.source_document: Physio - القسم.pdf, p. 13

explanations.explanation_text: The majority of storage iron (ferritin/hemosiderin) is located in the liver (hepatocytes and Kupffer cells), with smaller amounts in the spleen and bone marrow.
explanations.source_document: Physio - القسم.pdf, p. 12

explanations.explanation_text: High altitude causes low atmospheric oxygen tension and systemic tissue hypoxia, which stimulates renal erythropoietin production and accelerates erythropoiesis, leading to polycythemia.
explanations.source_document: Physio - القسم.pdf, p. 11; Histo - القسم.pdf, p. 7

explanations.explanation_text: Vitamin K is required for the hepatic synthesis of blood clotting factors (prothrombin group), not for erythropoiesis.
explanations.source_document: Physio - القسم.pdf, pp. 11, 27; Histo - القسم.pdf, p. 7

explanations.explanation_text: After age 20, red marrow in the shafts of long bones is replaced by inactive yellow marrow; erythropoiesis becomes confined to flat and irregular bones.
explanations.source_document: Physio - القسم.pdf, p. 9; Histo - القسم.pdf, p. 19

explanations.explanation_text: Hepatic hemopoiesis ceases at about the time of birth; the liver does not produce red blood cells during the first 5 years of life.
explanations.source_document: Physio - القسم.pdf, p. 9; Histo - القسم.pdf, p. 20

explanations.explanation_text: African trypanosomes are obligate extracellular bloodstream and tissue fluid flagellates; they do not hide intracellularly in the vertebrate host.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (1) 2027 para.pdf, printed pp. 64, 69 (PDF pp. 69, 74)

explanations.explanation_text: The anterior (ventral) root contains motor (efferent) nerve fibers supplying skeletal muscles and autonomic effectors, not ascending sensory fibers.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 238

explanations.explanation_text: The human spinal cord gives rise to 31 pairs of spinal nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal), not 29 pairs.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 232, 238

explanations.explanation_text: The mature human umbilical cord contains only ONE functional umbilical vein (the left umbilical vein, carrying oxygen-rich blood from placenta to fetus), as the right umbilical vein undergoes complete obliteration during early development.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 351, 356

explanations.explanation_text: The normal umbilical cord possesses TWO umbilical arteries (which return deoxygenated fetal blood to the placenta); the presence of a single umbilical artery is an abnormal congenital variant.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 351, 356, 363

explanations.explanation_text: The nuclear envelope is composed of two concentric parallel unit membranes (inner and outer nuclear membranes) interrupted at multiple circular junctions where the inner and outer membranes fuse to form nuclear pores that regulate nucleocytoplasmic macromolecular transport.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 16 (PDF p. 24)

explanations.explanation_text: Under light microscopy, the nuclear envelope appears as a thin basophilic line owing to the layer of heterochromatin attached to its inner membrane and ribosomes studding its outer membrane, not an acidophilic line.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 15 (PDF p. 23)

explanations.explanation_text: The outer nuclear membrane is granular (studded with attached ribosomes continuous with the rER), whereas the inner nuclear membrane is fibrillar due to association with the nuclear lamina (intermediate lamin filaments) and peripheral chromatin.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 16 (PDF p. 24)

explanations.explanation_text: Statement A is an established, correct histological fact.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 16 (PDF p. 24)

explanations.explanation_text: Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) is a chemical histochemical stain applied to fixed tissue sections to demonstrate carbohydrates, glycogen, and neutral mucins.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 4) & printed p. 19 (PDF p. 26)

explanations.explanation_text: Silver staining is a heavy metal impregnation method performed on dead, fixed tissues to highlight reticular fibers, neurons, or Golgi complexes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 4) & printed p. 5 (PDF p. 65)

explanations.explanation_text: India ink (or trypan blue) is the classic vital stain administered to living cells or animals; macrophages (histiocytes) actively ingest the insoluble carbon colloidal particles by phagocytosis, demonstrating their vital phagocytic activity in living tissues.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 4) & printed p. 5 (PDF p. 65)

explanations.explanation_text: Best's carmine is a post-fixation histochemical dye used on histology slides specifically to stain glycogen red.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 4) & printed p. 19 (PDF p. 26)

explanations.explanation_text: The ovary contains extensive lymphatic networks draining along the ovarian vessels to para-aortic lymph nodes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 245

explanations.explanation_text: The brain (and spinal cord) possesses no true lymphatic capillaries or vessels within its parenchyma; its interstitial fluid and waste are cleared via cerebrospinal fluid pathways.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 245

explanations.explanation_text: The stomach is richly endowed with intramural lymphatic channels draining into perigastric and celiac nodes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 245

explanations.explanation_text: The breast has an abundant, clinically significant lymphatic drainage network draining into axillary and internal mammary lymph nodes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 245

explanations.explanation_text: Wharton's jelly is the specialized gelatinous mucoid connective tissue matrix that surrounds and insulates the umbilical vessels throughout the cord, rich in glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans to prevent mechanical compression and vessel occlusion.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 11 (PDF p. 71) & PDF pp. 351, 356

explanations.explanation_text: The umbilical cord attaches to the fetal surface of the placenta, typically near the center, and connects the fetus to the chorionic plate, never directly to the maternal decidual surface.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 331, 332

explanations.explanation_text: The decidua is the functional layer of the uterine endometrium during pregnancy, specially modified following blastocyst implantation by the maternal decidual reaction (stromal cells swell with glycogen and lipids, glandular secretions increase, and vascularity expands).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 280

explanations.explanation_text: The muscular wall of the uterus is the myometrium, composed of interlacing bundles of smooth muscle fibers, not the decidua.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 344

explanations.explanation_text: The outermost extraembryonic fetal membrane is the chorion (composed of trophoblast and extraembryonic somatic mesoderm), not the maternal decidua.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 285

explanations.explanation_text: The protective fluid surrounding the developing embryo inside the amniotic cavity is the amniotic fluid, not decidua.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 348

explanations.explanation_text: The glycocalyx (cell coat) is a carbohydrate-rich fuzzy surface coating present exclusively on the external leaflet of the plasma membrane, formed of oligosaccharide chains covalently bound to membrane proteins (glycoproteins) and lipids (glycolipids), functioning in cell recognition, adhesion, and receptor activity.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 12)

explanations.explanation_text: By day 14 of intrauterine life (the end of the second week), the extraembryonic coelom expands to form the chorionic cavity, and the trophoblast together with underlying extraembryonic somatic mesoderm forms the chorion, thereby transforming the blastocyst into the definitive chorionic vesicle.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 285, 288

explanations.explanation_text: By day 14 of intrauterine life (the end of the second week), the extraembryonic coelom expands to form the chorionic cavity, and the trophoblast together with underlying extraembryonic somatic mesoderm forms the chorion, thereby transforming the blastocyst into the definitive chorionic vesicle.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 271, 272

explanations.explanation_text: By day 14 of intrauterine life (the end of the second week), the extraembryonic coelom expands to form the chorionic cavity, and the trophoblast together with underlying extraembryonic somatic mesoderm forms the chorion, thereby transforming the blastocyst into the definitive chorionic vesicle.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 272, 274

explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 281, 282, 283

explanations.explanation_text: Ribosomes attached to the rER synthesize proteins destined for secretion, incorporation into lysosomes, or insertion into cellular membranes, not soluble cytoskeletal actin.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 7 (PDF p. 15) & printed p. 12 (PDF p. 20)

explanations.explanation_text: Lysosomes are digestive organelles containing acid hydrolases; they degrade cellular components rather than synthesizing cytoskeletal proteins.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 18)

explanations.explanation_text: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum is enzymatically dedicated to lipid/steroid metabolism, having no translational machinery for protein synthesis.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: Infiltration of chorionic villi into the myometrium defines placenta accreta/increta, not omphalocele.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 344

explanations.explanation_text: Omphalocele is a congenital umbilical hernia where abdominal viscera remain herniated into the base of the umbilical cord due to failure of gut loop retraction during the 10th week, covered by an amnion-peritoneal sac.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 357, 362

explanations.explanation_text: Rupture of the amniotic sac prior to labor defines premature rupture of membranes (PROM).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 350

explanations.explanation_text: Attachment of umbilical vessels through the amniochorionic membrane defines velamentous cord insertion.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 342, 357

explanations.explanation_text: Hypnozoite dormancy in hepatocytes is clinically silent and causes no fever until reactivation occurs.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (1) 2027 para.pdf, printed p. 35 (PDF p. 40)

explanations.explanation_text: Articular surfaces of synovial joints are capped by hyaline cartilage, which provides a smooth, frictionless bearing surface.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 77) & PDF p. 113

explanations.explanation_text: White fibrocartilage is characteristically found in the intervertebral discs (annulus fibrosus) and the pubic symphysis, where thick parallel bundles of type I collagen confer immense resistance to compression and shearing forces.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 77) & PDF p. 114

explanations.explanation_text: The pinna (auricle) of the ear is formed of yellow elastic cartilage, rich in elastic fibers to maintain structural shape while allowing flexible bending.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 77) & PDF p. 115

explanations.explanation_text: The cartilaginous framework of the external nose is composed of hyaline cartilage, not fibrocartilage.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 77) & PDF p. 113

explanations.explanation_text: The luminal mucosa of the small intestine is lined by simple columnar epithelium possessing thousands of densely packed apical microvilli that form a prominent brush (striated) border under the light microscope to dramatically amplify the absorptive surface area.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 43) & printed p. 5 (PDF p. 57)

explanations.explanation_text: The trachea is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, featuring motile cilia rather than absorptive microvillous brush borders.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 44)

explanations.explanation_text: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium) characterized by dome-shaped umbrella cells without a brush border.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 46)

explanations.explanation_text: The esophagus is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium designed to protect against mechanical bolus abrasion.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 5 (PDF p. 45)

explanations.explanation_text: Osteocytes are mature bone cells that become trapped within small oval matrix spaces known as lacunae during osteogenesis, communicating with neighboring lacunae via branching canaliculi.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3–4 (PDF pp. 83–84)

explanations.explanation_text: Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells located on bone surfaces within shallow enzymatically excavated depressions called Howship's lacunae (resorption bays), not within enclosed interstitial bone matrix lacunae.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 84)

explanations.explanation_text: Fibroblasts are the primary cells of connective tissue proper, found embedded within loose or dense connective tissue stroma, and do not reside in lacunae.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 64)

explanations.explanation_text: The decidua is the maternal functional endometrium of the pregnant uterus following implantation of the blastocyst, containing decidual stromal cells that have accumulated glycogen and lipids to support early embryonic nutrition and control trophoblast invasion. Incorrect: Abnormal attachment of the umbilical cord describes cord insertion anomalies (such as velamentous or battledore insertion), not the decidua.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 280

explanations.explanation_text: In muscle fibers, the smooth endoplasmic reticulum is specialized as the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which contains active ATP-dependent calcium pumps (SERCA) that sequester calcium ions during relaxation and release them into the sarcoplasm to trigger muscle contraction.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: Protein synthesis is carried out by ribosomes (free or bound to rER); the smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and cannot synthesize proteins.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: The defining morphological feature of smooth endoplasmic reticulum is the complete absence of ribosomes on its tubular membrane surface.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: Statement A is an established, correct histological fact.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: During normal embryonic development, physiological umbilical herniation occurs at the 6th week because the rapidly growing midgut loop outgrows the abdominal cavity, entering the extraembryonic coelom within the umbilical cord, and then normally returns to the abdominal cavity by the 10th week (during the 3rd month).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 355, 356

explanations.explanation_text: Normal development involves degeneration of the right umbilical vein and persistence of the left umbilical vein, not the reverse.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 356

explanations.explanation_text: Wharton's jelly is formed by transformation of the extraembryonic mesoderm of the connecting stalk, not from surface ectoderm.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 356

explanations.explanation_text: Statement A is an established embryological fact.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 355, 356

explanations.explanation_text: Rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is dedicated to the synthesis and segregation of proteins destined for export, membranes, or lysosomes via attached ribosomes, having no metabolic role in xenobiotic detoxification.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 7 (PDF p. 15)

explanations.explanation_text: The Golgi apparatus modifies, terminal-glycosylates, packages, and sorts secretory products, rather than detoxifying chemical compounds.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 9 (PDF p. 17)

explanations.explanation_text: Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases that degrade endocytosed and autophagocytosed macromolecules and cellular debris, not microsomal drug-metabolizing enzymes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 18)

explanations.explanation_text: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) in hepatocytes is packed with cytochrome P450 monooxygenases and conjugating enzymes that chemically oxidize, hydroxylate, and detoxify drugs, alcohol, barbiturates, steroid hormones, and hydrophobic toxic metabolites.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: Fertilization of two distinct ova by two sperms causes dizygotic (fraternal) twins, which develop completely separate fetuses and fetal membranes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 365, 368, 369

explanations.explanation_text: Two separate blastocysts implanting in close proximity can result in fused placentas, but their embryonic bodies remain entirely separate and never develop into conjoined twins.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 368

explanations.explanation_text: Fused (conjoined or Siamese) twins result from the incomplete or partial splitting of the inner cell mass or embryonic disc in a monozygotic pregnancy after day 13, producing twins joined at anatomical regions such as the thorax (thoracopagus), head (craniopagus), or pelvis (pygopagus).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 367, 371–373

explanations.explanation_text: Polyspermy (fertilization of an ovum by more than one sperm) results in triploidy (69 chromosomes), which causes hydatidiform molar change or early embryonic lethality, not viable conjoined twins.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 38) & PDF p. 266

explanations.explanation_text: Macrophages (histiocytes) are motile or fixed phagocytic cells that roam the connective tissue matrix or line sinusoids, lacking any surrounding rigid lacunar spaces.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 5 (PDF p. 65)

explanations.explanation_text: Gastrulation is the defining formative process of the third week of embryonic development whereby the bilaminar embryonic disc (composed of epiblast and hypoblast) is transformed into a trilaminar embryonic disc composed of all three primary germ layers: ectoderm, intraembryonic mesoderm, and endoderm.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 285, 291, 292

explanations.explanation_text: Formation of the morula (a solid sphere of 16 blastomeres) occurs on day 3–4 after fertilization via early mitotic cleavage divisions in the uterine tube.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 269, 270

explanations.explanation_text: In response to antigenic challenge or infection, activated lymphocytes undergo rapid clonal expansion and blast transformation in the germinal centers (lymphoid hyperplasia), causing noticeable enlargement (swelling) of the lymph node.
explanations.source_document: Histo - القسم.pdf, pp. 27, 30; Micro - القسم.pdf, printed p. 151 (PDF p. 154)

explanations.explanation_text: Mitochondria are the "powerhouses of the cell", containing the enzymes of the Krebs citric acid cycle in their matrix and the respiratory electron transport chain complexes on their cristae to generate cellular energy stored as adenosine triphosphate (ATP) through aerobic oxidation.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 6–7 (PDF pp. 14–15)

explanations.explanation_text: The Golgi apparatus is the secretory packaging center, not an ATP-producing energy organelle.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8–9 (PDF pp. 16–17)

explanations.explanation_text: The nucleolus is the site of rRNA synthesis and ribosome assembly.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 17 (PDF p. 25)

explanations.explanation_text: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes lipids and steroids and detoxifies compounds, consuming rather than generating ATP.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: Fertilization normally takes place in the ampulla of the uterine tube, which is the expanded, thin-walled lateral third of the fallopian tube.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 263

explanations.explanation_text: Statement C is an established embryological fact.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 263

explanations.explanation_text: The first week of development is characterized by fertilization, cleavage divisions of the zygote, morula formation, blastocyst cavitation, and initiation of implantation on day 6.

explanations.explanation_text: 27 microtubules arranged as 9 triplets (9x3 = 27 MTs) is the exact ultrastructural composition of the basal body and centriole, not the ciliary shaft. 18 microtubules represent only the 9 peripheral doublets (9x2 = 18 MTs) of the axoneme, omitting the 2 central singlet microtubules. The axoneme (shaft) of a motile cilium is composed of precisely 20 microtubules arranged in the classic 9+2 configuration: 9 peripheral doublets (9x2 = 18 MTs) encircling 2 central singlet microtubules (18 + 2 = 20 MTs), all enveloped by the apical plasma membrane. Incorrect: 9 microtubules do not represent any complete ciliary subcomponent.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 14 (PDF p. 22) & printed p. 7 (PDF p. 59)

explanations.explanation_text: The sartorius is an example of a long, strap-like (parallel-fibered) muscle that runs obliquely across the anterior compartment of the thigh.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 168, 170

explanations.explanation_text: Orbicularis oris is a circular muscle that encircles the oral fissure, functioning as an oral sphincter to close, compress, and protrude the lips.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 170

explanations.explanation_text: The rectus abdominis is a long, vertical, strap-like muscle featuring transverse tendinous intersections (intersections tendineae) in the anterior abdominal wall.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 170

explanations.explanation_text: The temporalis is a broad, fan-shaped (convergent/radiate) masticatory muscle arising from the temporal fossa and converging onto the coronoid process of the mandible.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 129, 170

explanations.explanation_text: The hip joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket synovial joint providing three degrees of freedom (flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, and medial/lateral rotation).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 157, 161, 168

explanations.explanation_text: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is a biaxial ellipsoid synovial joint permitting movements around two orthogonal axes (flexion/extension and abduction/adduction).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 157, 160

explanations.explanation_text: Interphalangeal joints are uniaxial hinge (ginglymus) joints operating around a transverse axis, permitting only flexion and extension.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 157, 159

explanations.explanation_text: Rapidly dividing proliferating cells dilute cytoplasmic contents during cytokinesis and do not accumulate lipofuscin.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 18)

explanations.explanation_text: Excessive lipid synthesis leads to neutral triglyceride droplet accumulation (steatosis or lipid droplets), not autofluorescent lipofuscin pigments.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 19 (PDF p. 26)

explanations.explanation_text: Lipofuscin ("wear-and-tear" or aging pigment) is a fine yellow-brown intracellular inclusion composed of lipid-containing residues of lysosomal digestion, accumulating as a direct consequence of cumulative oxidative stress, free-radical damage, and cellular aging in long-lived post-mitotic cells (cardiac myocytes and neurons).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 18) & printed p. 19 (PDF p. 26)

explanations.explanation_text: Viral infections produce diagnostic viral inclusion bodies (nuclear or cytoplasmic protein aggregates), not endogenous lipofuscin granules.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 19 (PDF p. 26)

explanations.explanation_text: Bilateral renal agenesis (Potter's syndrome) or severe obstructive uropathy abolishes fetal urine production (micturition), which is the primary contributor to amniotic fluid volume during the second and third trimesters, directly resulting in severe oligohydramnios.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 349

explanations.explanation_text: Sutures are fibrous joints restricted entirely to the flat bones of the skull, where articulating bone edges are united by thin sutural ligaments that ossify with age.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 150

explanations.explanation_text: A gomphosis (peg-and-socket fibrous joint) is the specialized fibrous articulation between the conical root of each tooth and its corresponding bony alveolar socket in the maxilla or mandible, anchored securely by the periodontal ligament.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 150

explanations.explanation_text: A syndesmosis is a fibrous joint in which opposing bones are united by a substantial interosseous ligament or membrane (such as the inferior tibiofibular joint or interosseous membrane of forearm/leg), allowing slight give.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 150

explanations.explanation_text: Synovial joints are freely mobile joints enclosed by a fibrous capsule lined by synovial membrane and containing synovial fluid; they are not found anchoring teeth into alveolar sockets.

explanations.explanation_text: Intervertebral discs are formed of white fibrocartilage (the peripheral annulus fibrosus) and a central gelatinous nucleus pulposus, not yellow elastic connective tissue.

explanations.explanation_text: Costal cartilages connecting the ribs to the sternum are composed of hyaline cartilage, not elastic connective tissue.

explanations.explanation_text: Tendons of muscles are composed of dense regular collagenous connective tissue, characterized by parallel bundles of type I collagen fibers.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 70)

explanations.explanation_text: Yellow elastic connective tissue consists predominantly of thick, branching, parallel elastic fibers, and is characteristically found in the ligamentum nuchae (at the back of the neck), ligamenta flava of the vertebral column, and the walls of large elastic arteries.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 11 (PDF p. 71)

explanations.explanation_text: Type II collagen fibers are specific to the matrix of hyaline and elastic cartilages, providing tensile resistance to swelling pressure, and are absent in mature bone matrix.

explanations.explanation_text: The ovary possesses a rich intrinsic lymphatic network within its cortical stroma and medulla that drains into lymphatic vessels ascending along the ovarian blood vessels to terminate in the lateral aortic (para-aortic) and lumbar lymph nodes.

explanations.explanation_text: The central nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord, completely lacks true lymphatic capillaries and vessels.

explanations.explanation_text: Fibroblasts are resident connective tissue cells of mesenchymal lineage that synthesize extracellular fibers, having no lineage relationship to bone-resorbing osteoclasts.

explanations.explanation_text: The primordium of the central nervous system is the neural tube (induced by the notochord from overlying ectoderm), not the notochord itself.

explanations.explanation_text: Arteriovenous anastomoses are direct vascular shunts connecting small arterioles to venules without intervening capillary beds, functioning primarily in thermoregulation and hemodynamics.

explanations.explanation_text: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is the classic anatomical example of a biaxial ellipsoid (condyloid) synovial joint, where an oval convex surface (distal radius and articular disc) articulates with an elliptical concave surface (scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum), permitting flexion/extension and abduction/adduction (radial/ulnar deviation) as well as circumduction, but no axial rotation.

explanations.explanation_text: The elbow (humeroulnar and humeroradial) joint is a uniaxial hinge (ginglymus) joint that allows movement primarily in one transverse axis, namely flexion and extension.

explanations.explanation_text: The ankle (talocrural) joint is structurally a uniaxial hinge joint between the mortise of the distal tibia/fibula and the trochlea of the talus, allowing predominantly dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.

explanations.explanation_text: The knee joint is classified as a modified hinge or bicondylar complex synovial joint with intra-articular structures (menisci and cruciate ligaments), not an ellipsoid joint.

explanations.explanation_text: The palmar arches (superficial and deep palmar arches of the hand) and plantar arches of the foot represent classic end-to-end arterial anastomoses, where terminal branches of major parent arteries (radial/ulnar or medial/lateral plantar) join directly end-to-end to ensure uninterrupted distal circulation regardless of hand or foot posture.

explanations.explanation_text: Apoptosis is by definition programmed, genetically regulated, energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) cell death that affects individual scattered cells under physiological conditions (such as embryogenesis and tissue turnover) or pathological states, characterized by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis), and intact plasma membrane blebbing without inflammatory reaction.

explanations.explanation_text: The large intestine is lined by simple columnar epithelium with absorptive microvilli and abundant mucus-secreting goblet cells, and does NOT possess cilia. Although designated by the original exam answer key as option A, the reference handout clearly specifies that cilia are found in the respiratory tract and oviduct, not the large intestine. True cilia are active motile cell processes that undergo synchronized, rhythmic coordinated beating, unlike non-motile stereocilia or microvilli. The physiological function of motile cilia is to generate unidirectional, rhythmic beating movements that push and propel luminal fluids and particles (such as mucus carrying inhaled dust in the respiratory tract and the ovum toward the uterus in the oviduct). Incorrect: Increasing the apical surface area for absorption is the specific function of microvilli (and stereocilia), not motile cilia whose primary purpose is fluid/particle transport. Answer Key Conflict: Original exam answer: A. In large intestine

explanations.explanation_text: The lipid component of the membrane consists of the phospholipid bilayer and intercalated cholesterol molecules, which do not alone constitute the glycocalyx.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 12)

explanations.explanation_text: The glycocalyx is located strictly and exclusively on the external (extracellular) surface of the plasma membrane; it is completely absent from the inner cytoplasmic leaflet.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 12)

explanations.explanation_text: The glycocalyx is the carbohydrate-rich outer coat of the cell membrane composed of the oligosaccharide chains of glycolipids and glycoproteins projecting from the external leaflet of the lipid bilayer, functioning in cellular recognition, protection, and receptor display.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 12)

explanations.explanation_text: The superior (proximal) radio-ulnar joint is the classic pivot (trochoid) uniaxial synovial joint, in which the cylindrical head of the radius rotates within the fibro-osseous ring formed by the radial notch of the ulna and the annular ligament around a longitudinal axis, producing pronation and supination of the forearm.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 157, 159

explanations.explanation_text: Omphalocele is a major developmental abnormality in which abdominal viscera remain herniated into the proximal part of the umbilical cord.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 357, 362

explanations.explanation_text: Necrosis is unprogrammed, accidental pathological cell death affecting groups of adjacent cells caused by severe external mechanical, physical, or chemical injury, characterized by plasma membrane perforation, organelle swelling, lysis, and secondary acute inflammatory responses.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 30)

explanations.explanation_text: Inflammation is a complex vascular and cellular protective response of living vascularized tissue to injury or infection, not the definition of programmed cell death.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 30)

explanations.explanation_text: Metaplasia is a reversible adaptive replacement of one differentiated adult cell type by another differentiated cell type better suited to withstand chronic environmental stress.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 4 (PDF p. 30)

explanations.explanation_text: The epithelial parenchyma of the liver (hepatocytes and intrahepatic biliary epithelium) develops directly from the endodermal lining of the foregut via the hepatic diverticulum (liver bud).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 319

explanations.explanation_text: The skin has a dual origin: the outer epidermis is derived from surface ectoderm, while the underlying dermis is derived from paraxial mesoderm (dermatomes) and somatopleuric lateral plate mesoderm.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 308, 314

explanations.explanation_text: All muscular tissues (skeletal muscles from paraxial somitic myotomes, smooth muscles from splanchnopleuric mesoderm, and cardiac muscles from splanchnic mesoderm) originate from embryonic mesoderm, not endoderm.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 314, 318

explanations.explanation_text: Deep fascia is a dense, inelastic, fibrous collagenous membrane that is completely devoid of fat cells; it is the superficial fascia (subcutaneous tissue) that contains variable and abundant amounts of adipose tissue.

explanations.explanation_text: The tibia is classified morphologically as a long bone, possessing a shaft (diaphysis) and two expanded ends (epiphyses), located in the medial aspect of the leg.

explanations.explanation_text: The maxilla is a classic pneumatic bone; it contains large internal air-filled cavities (the maxillary paranasal sinuses) lined by mucous membrane that communicate with the nasal cavity to lighten the weight of the skull and provide voice resonance.

explanations.explanation_text: The scapula is classified as a flat bone, consisting of two thin plates of compact bone enclosing spongy bone (cancellous bone), located in the posterior thoracic wall.

explanations.explanation_text: Embryonic folding in both craniocaudal and lateral planes transforms the flat trilaminar embryonic disc into a distinct three-dimensional cylindrical shape containing an intraembryonic body cavity; therefore, this is an established result of folding.

explanations.explanation_text: During lateral and craniocaudal folding, the dorsal portion of the primary yolk sac is pinched and incorporated into the embryo to form the primitive gut, while the remainder is compressed into the definitive yolk sac connected via the vitelline duct; this structural division is a direct mechanical consequence of folding.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 326

explanations.explanation_text: The formation of the primitive gut tube (foregut, midgut, and hindgut) is one of the principal consequences of embryonic folding as the endodermal layer is enclosed within the cylindrical body wall.

explanations.explanation_text: In anaerobic glycolysis, 4 ATP are generated at substrate level (by phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase) and 2 ATP are consumed in the preparatory phase (by hexokinase and PFK-1), yielding a net gain of exactly 2 ATP per glucose molecule. The 2 NADH produced are re-oxidized by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+, so no ETC ATP is formed. Under aerobic conditions, re-oxidation of 2 cytosolic NADH by the ETC yields up to 5 ATP, but under anaerobic conditions NADH cannot be oxidized by mitochondria. Four ATP represents the gross substrate-level ATP generation before subtracting the 2 ATP invested in the activation reactions. Incorrect: Seven ATP represents the net energy yield of aerobic glycolysis (4 substrate ATP + 5 ETC ATP - 2 consumed ATP = 7 ATP).

explanations.explanation_text: Hemoglobin is a globular conjugated chromoprotein with very few disulfide bonds.

explanations.explanation_text: Keratin is a fibrous scleroprotein characterized by an exceptionally high content of cystine forming extensive disulfide bonds that confer rigidity and insolubility.

explanations.explanation_text: Facilitated diffusion relies on specific carrier proteins that exhibit saturation kinetics (Vmax) when all carrier binding sites are fully occupied.
explanations.source_document: NS 101 2027 part (2) physio.pdf, printed p. 20 (PDF p. 23)

explanations.explanation_text: Facilitated diffusion is a passive process that does not require cellular metabolic energy or ATP hydrolysis.

explanations.explanation_text: Facilitated diffusion strictly transports substances down their concentration gradient.

explanations.explanation_text: Gastrulation is the defining morphogenetic process of the third embryonic week by which the bilaminar embryonic disc (epiblast and hypoblast) is converted into a three-layered (trilaminar) disc composed of ectoderm, intraembryonic mesoderm, and endoderm through the primitive streak.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 291, 292

explanations.explanation_text: Ischemia-induced hypoxia impairs oxidative phosphorylation, depleting cellular ATP and opening the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP) in the inner mitochondrial membrane; the resulting increased inner membrane permeability dissipates the proton electrochemical gradient, abolishing ATP synthase activity and causing influx of water and solutes that produces high-amplitude mitochondrial swelling and cristae disruption.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 6–7 (PDF pp. 14–15)

explanations.explanation_text: Blood coagulation requires Vitamin K, which serves as a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase activating clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, whereas Vitamin A is primarily involved in vision and epithelial differentiation.
explanations.source_document: Bio - القسم.pdf, printed p. 14 (PDF p. 16)

explanations.explanation_text: Osteomalacia and rickets are caused by deficiency of Vitamin D (and calcium), whereas Vitamin A deficiency causes ocular and epithelial manifestations.
explanations.source_document: Bio - القسم.pdf, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 12)

explanations.explanation_text: Best's carmine is a specialized histological stain that selectively binds and stains cytoplasmic glycogen granules bright red/magenta, making it a classic histochemical method for visualizing glycogen in hepatocytes and muscle fibers. (Note: Periodic acid–Schiff [PAS] is also used; in this exam, Best's carmine is the designated key answer).

explanations.explanation_text: Silver impregnation techniques (such as reticulin silver stains) are used to visualize reticular fibers, Golgi apparatus, and neurofibrils, not glycogen.

explanations.explanation_text: While PAS also stains glycogen (and glycoproteins/mucins) magenta, Best's carmine is the specific selective carmine-based dye highlighted for glycogen demonstration in the curriculum.

explanations.explanation_text: India ink is a non-toxic particulate vital stain phagocytosed by reticuloendothelial macrophages (histiocytes) to demonstrate phagocytic capacity, not a glycogen stain.

explanations.explanation_text: Vitamin A deficiency leads to epithelial hyperkeratinization, manifesting clinically as dry, rough skin with follicular hyperkeratosis ('toad skin') and mucosal atrophy.

explanations.explanation_text: Vitamin A and carotenoids act as antioxidants and cellular differentiating agents that help prevent malignant transformation, rather than increasing cancer rates.

explanations.explanation_text: Option A is the correct exam answer because chondrocytes are mature cartilage cells embedded entirely within the lacunae of the cartilage extracellular matrix; they are NEVER found residing inside the perichondrium.

explanations.explanation_text: Undifferentiated mesenchymal cells (UMCs) and chondrogenic stem cells reside in the inner cellular (chondrogenic) layer of the perichondrium.

explanations.explanation_text: Chondroblasts differentiate from chondrogenic cells in the inner cellular layer of the perichondrium to participate in appositional cartilage growth.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 76)

explanations.explanation_text: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) deficiency causes classic galactosemia, the most common and severe form.
explanations.source_document: Bio - القسم.pdf, printed p. 66 (PDF p. 68)

explanations.explanation_text: Fibroblasts are the predominant cells located in the outer fibrous layer of the perichondrium, where they synthesize collagen fibers.

explanations.explanation_text: The tibialis anterior is the classic anatomical example of a circumpennate muscle, where muscle fibers converge circularly from all directions onto a central axial tendon, resembling a circular feather.

explanations.explanation_text: The sartorius is a strap-like (parallel-fibered) muscle, not pennate.

explanations.explanation_text: The temporalis is a radiate (convergent/fan-shaped) muscle.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 170

explanations.explanation_text: The rectus abdominis is a strap-like muscle with tendinous intersections.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 170

explanations.explanation_text: Phase 1 of fertilization is the penetration of the corona radiata, whereas Phase 2 represents the penetration of the zona pellucida.

explanations.explanation_text: The morula forms while still strictly enclosed within the intact protective zona pellucida (which prevents premature tubal implantation); the zona pellucida degenerates only at the late blastocyst stage (day 5–6).

explanations.explanation_text: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency causes Von Gierke's glycogen storage disease (Type I), NOT galactosemia; it is an enzyme of gluconeogenesis and glycogen breakdown.

explanations.explanation_text: In adult hemoglobin (HbA), the alpha-globin chain consists of exactly 141 amino acid residues folded into 7 helices or loops (helices A through G).

explanations.explanation_text: Each dimer contains one alpha and one beta chain (alphabeta), and two dimers associate to form the complete tetramer (alpha2beta2); an individual dimer is dimeric, not tetrameric on its own.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (2) 2027 bio.pdf, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 5)

explanations.explanation_text: Each polypeptide globin chain binds exactly ONE molecule of heme (four heme groups per whole tetrameric hemoglobin molecule, not 4 heme per chain).

explanations.explanation_text: Ribosomes are non-membranous ribonucleoprotein organelles completely devoid of any surrounding lipid bilayer membrane.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 11) & printed p. 12 (PDF p. 20)

explanations.explanation_text: Mitochondria are double-membrane-bound organelles bounded by an outer mitochondrial membrane (which is smooth and porous to small metabolites) and a selectively permeable inner mitochondrial membrane thrown into cristae.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 14)

explanations.explanation_text: Lysosomes are spherical organelles enveloped by a single unit membrane, not possessing an "outer" versus "inner" membrane arrangement.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 18)

explanations.explanation_text: The Golgi apparatus consists of stacks of curved, single-membrane-bound saccules (cisternae), lacking an outer/inner concentric double-membrane envelope.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 9 (PDF p. 17)

explanations.explanation_text: Klinefelter syndrome is a sex chromosome abnormality (47, XXY) resulting in tall stature and primary hypogonadism, not trisomy 21.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 38)

explanations.explanation_text: Turner syndrome is a sex chromosome monosomy (45, X0) in females, characterized by short stature and ovarian dysgenesis.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 38)

explanations.explanation_text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is caused by the presence of an extra chromosome 21 resulting from meiotic nondisjunction, characterized by distinct epicanthal folds, single palmar crease, intellectual disability, and hypotonia.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 38)

explanations.explanation_text: The auricle (pinna) of the external ear is composed of yellow elastic cartilage.

explanations.explanation_text: Costal cartilages (attaching the anterior ends of the ribs to the sternum) are composed of hyaline cartilage, characterized by a glassy homogeneous matrix containing type II collagen.

explanations.explanation_text: Intervertebral discs are formed of white fibrocartilage, specialized to resist heavy axial compressive loading.

explanations.explanation_text: Circulating blood monocytes migrate across postcapillary venules into the loose connective tissue stroma, where they enlarge, express surface pattern recognition receptors, expand their lysosomal system, and differentiate into fixed connective tissue macrophages known as histiocytes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 63) & printed p. 5 (PDF p. 65)

explanations.explanation_text: Undifferentiated mesenchymal cells (UMCs) are primitive multipotent stem cells that give rise to fibroblasts, chondroblasts, osteoblasts, and adipocytes, but the immediate precursor of connective tissue histiocytes is the blood monocyte.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 63)

explanations.explanation_text: Neutrophils are short-lived polymorphonuclear granular leukocytes involved in acute bacterial phagocytosis; they do not transform into histiocytes.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 63)

explanations.explanation_text: Plasma cells are differentiated terminal effector cells derived from activated B lymphocytes specialized exclusively for immunoglobulin (antibody) production.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 6 (PDF p. 66)

explanations.explanation_text: During prophase, as chromatin undergoes progressive condensation and RNA transcription stops, the nucleolus disassembles, disperses its constituent ribonucleoprotein subunits, and disappears from microscopic view.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 33)

explanations.explanation_text: By metaphase, the nucleolus is already completely absent, and chromosomes are maximally condensed and aligned at the spindle equator.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 33)

explanations.explanation_text: During anaphase, sister chromatids migrate to opposite poles in a cell completely devoid of a nucleolus.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 33)

explanations.explanation_text: During telophase, the nucleolus reassembles and reappears at the nucleolar organizer regions (NORs) of the reforming daughter nuclei.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 3 (PDF p. 33)

explanations.explanation_text: The ovary is the gonad responsible for folliculogenesis and ovulation of the secondary oocyte into the peritoneal cavity; fertilization does not occur within the ovarian stroma.

explanations.explanation_text: The presence of two umbilical arteries (accompanied by one umbilical vein) is the normal vascular anatomy of the definitive human umbilical cord, whereas having a single umbilical artery is the abnormal variant.

explanations.explanation_text: Ivermectin is the true, correct drug of choice for the treatment of onchocerciasis (Onchocerca volvulus river blindness).
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (1) 2027 para.pdf, printed p. 31 (PDF p. 36)

explanations.explanation_text: Quinine is a potent blood schizonticide that controls the acute clinical erythrocytic paroxysm, but it has no activity against dormant liver hypnozoites.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (1) 2027 para.pdf, printed p. 47 (PDF p. 52)

explanations.explanation_text: Chloroquine rapidly terminates the erythrocytic cycle for clinical cure but does not eliminate liver hypnozoites, so relapses still occur.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (1) 2027 para.pdf, printed p. 47 (PDF p. 52)

explanations.explanation_text: Tafenoquine (and primaquine) are 8-aminoquinolines that act as tissue schizonticides, directly eradicating the dormant liver hypnozoite forms of P. vivax and P. ovale to achieve radical cure.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (1) 2027 para.pdf, printed p. 47 (PDF p. 52)

explanations.explanation_text: Artemisinin combination therapies (ACT) are potent blood schizonticides used for clinical attacks and chloroquine-resistant malaria, but they do not eradicate hypnozoites.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (1) 2027 para.pdf, printed pp. 47, 48 (PDF pp. 52, 53)

explanations.explanation_text: Option A is INCORRECT (and therefore the correct answer): cephalosporins share the beta-lactam nucleus and exhibit immunological cross-reactivity with penicillins; they should NOT be routinely used in patients with severe penicillin allergy/anaphylaxis.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed p. 34 (PDF p. 37)

explanations.explanation_text: Certain cephalosporins (e.g. moxalactam, cefamandole, cefoperazone) contain a methylthiotetrazole ring that inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed p. 35 (PDF p. 38)

explanations.explanation_text: First-generation cephalosporins do not cross the blood-brain barrier into the CSF in adequate amounts, which is why 3rd-generation agents are preferred for meningitis.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed p. 34 (PDF p. 37)

explanations.explanation_text: Doxycycline reversibly binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks the attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosomal acceptor (A) site, halting polypeptide elongation.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed p. 38 (PDF p. 41)

explanations.explanation_text: Doxycycline is a PROTEIN SYNTHESIS INHIBITOR acting on the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit; it does NOT inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed pp. 29, 37, 38 (PDF pp. 32, 40, 41)

explanations.explanation_text: Bacitracin is a cell wall synthesis inhibitor that prevents dephosphorylation of the lipid carrier molecule.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed pp. 29, 36 (PDF pp. 32, 39)

explanations.explanation_text: Cycloserine is a structural analog of D-alanine that inhibits cell wall synthesis enzymes.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed pp. 29, 36 (PDF pp. 32, 39)

explanations.explanation_text: Cephalosporins are beta-lactam antibiotics that inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking in the bacterial cell wall.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (4) 2027-pharma.pdf, printed pp. 29, 34 (PDF pp. 32, 37)

explanations.explanation_text: Burkitt lymphoma is classified as a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with an extremely rapid tumor proliferation rate and mitotic index.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (3) 2027 pathology.pdf, printed pp. 8, 11 (PDF pp. 9, 12)

explanations.explanation_text: Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells are the diagnostic neoplastic hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma, and are absent in non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (3) 2027 pathology.pdf, printed pp. 14, 17 (PDF pp. 15, 18)

explanations.explanation_text: Hodgkin lymphoma typically presents in cervical lymph nodes with contiguous spread, whereas NHL frequently presents with non-contiguous lymphadenopathy or extranodal disease.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (3) 2027 pathology.pdf, printed pp. 13, 17 (PDF pp. 14, 18)

explanations.explanation_text: Burkitt lymphoma is strongly linked to viral infection with Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and MYC gene translocation, not primary bacterial infection.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (3) 2027 pathology.pdf, printed p. 11 (PDF p. 12)

explanations.explanation_text: Secondary polycythemia develops as a physiological response to systemic hypoxia (e.g. chronic lung disease, high altitude, cyanotic heart disease) which stimulates renal erythropoietin production to drive bone marrow erythropoiesis.
explanations.source_document: HAEM 202 part (3) 2027 pathology.pdf, printed p. 18 (PDF p. 19)

explanations.explanation_text: A secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) is a permanent, slightly mobile midline joint united by a disc of fibrocartilage (such as the intervertebral discs and symphysis pubis).
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 151

explanations.explanation_text: The epiphyseal cartilage plate uniting the epiphysis to the diaphysis in a growing long bone is the classic primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis); it consists of a temporary plate of hyaline cartilage that is completely immobile and undergoes endochondral ossification (synostosis) upon cessation of growth.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF p. 151

explanations.explanation_text: A synovial joint possesses a fluid-filled cavity, fibrous capsule, and high mobility, which are completely absent in the solid epiphyseal growth plate.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 152, 153

explanations.explanation_text: A synovial joint possesses a fluid-filled cavity, fibrous capsule, and high mobility, which are completely absent in the solid epiphyseal growth plate.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 149, 150

explanations.explanation_text: Dense regular collagenous connective tissue (exemplified by tendons, aponeuroses, and corneal stroma) is histologically characterized by densely packed, thick bundles of type I collagen arranged in strict, parallel orientation to withstand unidirectional tensile forces, with flattened, inactive fibroblasts (fibrocytes / tendon cells) compressed in rows between the bundles.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 70) & printed p. 12 (PDF p. 72)

explanations.explanation_text: Dense irregular connective tissue (such as the dermis and organ capsules) consists of coarse collagen bundles woven randomly in all spatial directions without parallel alignment.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 10 (PDF p. 70) & printed p. 12 (PDF p. 72)

explanations.explanation_text: Loose areolar connective tissue contains an abundance of amorphous ground substance, a wide variety of wandering and fixed cells, and a loose, randomly distributed meshwork of thin fibers.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 11 (PDF p. 71) & printed p. 12 (PDF p. 72)

explanations.explanation_text: Reticular connective tissue is formed of delicate, branching networks of type III collagen (reticular fibers) associated with stellate reticular cells, forming the soft stroma of lymphoid and hemopoietic organs.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, printed p. 11 (PDF p. 71) & printed p. 12 (PDF p. 72)

explanations.explanation_text: The spinal cord gives rise to 31 pairs of spinal nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal), not 29.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 232, 238

explanations.explanation_text: The anterior root carries somatic motor fibers to skeletal muscles and autonomic preganglionic fibers to viscera, not ascending sensory fibers.
explanations.source_document: Normal Structure II Handout, PDF pp. 238, 241
